explanations.answer: There is no resurrection of the dead
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says some in Corinth were saying there is no resurrection of the dead, even though it's preached that Christ has been raised (1 Corinthians 15:12). He asks how both can be true. It's like praising my cookies while swearing I don't own an oven.

Paul doesn't say anyone in Corinth claimed that. The claim in this verse is about the dead rising. Earlier in this same letter, Paul passes along “…that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,” (1 Corinthians 15:4). Burial isn't the argument here, friend. Rising is.

explanations.answer: Paul is not a real apostle
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't bring that up anywhere in these verses. The only thing he pushes back on is what some are saying about the resurrection of the dead. Nobody's checking his business card in this passage, friend. They're arguing about what happens to the dead.

Paul says the opposite, friend. His words are “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.” (1 Corinthians 15:13). He ties the two together so tightly you can't keep one and toss the other. It's like trying to take the chocolate chips back out of a baked cookie.

Right, and here's why. Paul says, “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.” (1 Corinthians 15:13). He won't let anybody split the two apart. If nobody rises, then Christ didn't either.
Paul says, “…our preaching is worthless…” (1 Corinthians 15:14). Everything the apostles proclaimed leans on Christ being raised. Without that, it's a cookie box with nothing inside, friend.
Paul says, “…and so is your faith.” (1 Corinthians 15:14). The Corinthians' own faith rests on the same thing the apostles' preaching does. If Christ has not been raised, both go down together.

Fasting is a fine word, but it didn't make Paul's list. In this verse, the two things that become worthless are the apostles' preaching and the Corinthians' faith (1 Corinthians 15:14). Paul is talking about what they proclaim and what they trust.

Paul doesn't mention giving here, friend. He says that if Christ has not been raised, the apostles' preaching is worthless, and so is the Corinthians' faith (1 Corinthians 15:14). Those are the two he names.

I'd love a good song as much as the next stamper, but singing isn't what Paul names. He says the preaching is worthless, and so is the faith (1 Corinthians 15:14). Those two are the ones hanging on Christ being raised.

Exactly. Paul says they would be “exposed as false witnesses about God” (1 Corinthians 15:15). They testified that God raised Christ from the dead. If the dead are not raised, then He didn't raise Him, and their testimony would be false.
That phrase shows up in Scripture, but not here. Jesus used “blind guides” in Matthew 23:16. Paul's words in this verse are about being false witnesses about God (1 Corinthians 15:15).

That's a picture from Jesus, friend, about a foolish man who built his house on sand (Matthew 7:26). Paul doesn't use it here. What he says is that they'd be exposed as false witnesses about God (1 Corinthians 15:15).

Yes, futile is Paul's word. He says, “And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile…” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Faith with nothing underneath it gets you nowhere, like stamping dough that never goes in the oven.
That's the opposite of Paul's point, friend. He says that if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). Nothing about growing in that sentence.
Paul doesn't say their faith would be hidden. He says it would be futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). Hidden is where I used to be, friend. Futile is the word on the page.

That's what he says. “…you are still in your sins.” (1 Corinthians 15:17). If Christ has not been raised, the Corinthians haven't been freed from them. That's the weight Paul puts on the resurrection.
Paul doesn't say that, friend. He says they would be still in their sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). His concern is where they stand, not whether they get cut off from anybody.
Doubts aren't the word Paul uses. He says, “…you are still in your sins.” (1 Corinthians 15:17). That's more serious than being confused, and it's what he spells out.

Paul says it the other way around, friend. If Christ has not been raised, then those who have fallen asleep in Christ “have perished” (1 Corinthians 15:18). He's not describing a safe rest there. He's spelling out how much hangs on the resurrection.

Right, Paul doesn't call it a safe rest. He says that if Christ has not been raised, those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished (1 Corinthians 15:18). It's one of the heaviest lines in this stretch. Hold on to the next part, because Paul turns it around.

explanations.answer: They should be pitied more than anyone
explanations.explanation: That's his line. “If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.” (1 Corinthians 15:19). Hoping in Christ for this life alone would leave them with nothing to look forward to. Paul is showing how much rides on the resurrection.

explanations.answer: They should be envied more than anyone
explanations.explanation: Envied is the opposite of what Paul says, friend. He says that if their hope in Christ is for this life alone, they are to be pitied more than all men (1 Corinthians 15:19). Nobody's lining up to trade places with that.

explanations.answer: They should be feared more than anyone
explanations.explanation: Paul never says fear here. He says they would be pitied more than all men (1 Corinthians 15:19). Pity is what you feel for someone left holding a hope with nothing behind it.

explanations.answer: He is the first of many to be raised
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), so more follow Him. Paul says so in verse 23: “…then at His coming, those who belong to Him.” (1 Corinthians 15:23). He goes first, and others come after.

explanations.answer: He is the only one ever to be raised
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite, friend. Firstfruits means there's more to follow, and he says, “…so in Christ all will be made alive.” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Christ goes first, not alone.

explanations.answer: He was the first person ever to die
explanations.explanation: The firstfruits picture is about being raised, not about dying. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, because He has been raised from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:20). He doesn't say Christ was the first to die.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, “For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man.” (1 Corinthians 15:21). Angels don't come into it. He keeps it man to man.
Right. Paul says the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man (1 Corinthians 15:21). Death came through a man, and so does the resurrection. No angels are part of that sentence.
Yes, Adam, the first man (Genesis 2:7). Paul says, “For as in Adam all die…” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Death came through him, and Paul is about to show who brings life.
Paul finishes the verse with, “…so in Christ all will be made alive.” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Death in one, life in the other. That's the whole turnaround in one sentence.
Moses, Israel's leader, is a great name, but Paul doesn't use him here. He puts Adam and Christ side by side (1 Corinthians 15:22). Those are the two men in the sentence.
Abraham, Israel's forefather, doesn't show up in this verse. Paul names Adam, through whom all die, and Christ, in whom all will be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22). Just those two.
Noah, the ark builder (Genesis 6:14-22), isn't in this verse, friend. Paul sets Adam against Christ (1 Corinthians 15:22). Those are the two names that matter here.

explanations.answer: Those who belong to Him at His coming
explanations.explanation: That's Paul's order. “…Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.” (1 Corinthians 15:23). He gives the order, not the date. My ovens just stay ready, because no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36).

explanations.answer: Everyone on earth the very next day
explanations.explanation: Paul gives no day at all. He says each in his own turn, then at His coming, those who belong to Him (1 Corinthians 15:23). And Jesus says no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36).
Paul doesn't limit it to the apostles or to one city. He says, “…those who belong to Him.” (1 Corinthians 15:23). It's about everyone who belongs to Him, friend.

explanations.answer: Until all His enemies are under His feet
explanations.explanation: You've got it. “For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet.” (1 Corinthians 15:25). He reigns until the job is done. That's the whole picture, baker.

explanations.answer: Until the temple is rebuilt in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: No temple shows up in this verse, friend. Paul says Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). That's the point he gives.

explanations.answer: Until the last apostle has died
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says Christ must reign “until He has put all His enemies under His feet.” (1 Corinthians 15:25). The apostles aren't part of the countdown.
That's the one. “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Death goes last, and it goes down.
Sin is serious, friend, but it isn't the one Paul names here. He says, “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” (1 Corinthians 15:26). That's his answer.
Paul doesn't name Satan in this verse. He says the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26). That's the name on the page.

That's what he says. “And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.” (1 Corinthians 15:28). Paul ends the stretch on that note.

Paul actually says it, friend. When all things have been subjected to the Son, the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28). That's why this one is true.

He does ask it. “If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?” (1 Corinthians 15:29). That's one more question showing how much rides on the resurrection. Paul doesn't say more about it here, so I won't either.

Paul does ask that, friend. The text says, “If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?” (1 Corinthians 15:29). It's one more question he raises about the resurrection of the dead.
Paul says, “I face death every day, brothers…” (1 Corinthians 15:31). Every day, friend. That's a lot of mornings I'd be asking for a day off.
That's far too slow for Paul. He says he faces death every day, not every year (1 Corinthians 15:31). He's talking daily.
Paul doesn't mention the Sabbath here. He says, “I face death every day, brothers…” (1 Corinthians 15:31). Not a weekly thing, friend. Daily.

explanations.answer: Live it up since tomorrow we die
explanations.explanation: That's the saying Paul quotes: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” (1 Corinthians 15:32). He says that's how it would go if the dead are not raised. Without the resurrection, it would be the logical way to live.

explanations.answer: Work hard since the end is near
explanations.explanation: Not the line Paul quotes, friend. His line is, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” (1 Corinthians 15:32). That one isn't about working harder.

explanations.answer: Stay quiet since no one is listening
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. What he quotes is, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” (1 Corinthians 15:32). Staying quiet isn't in the sentence.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He tells them, “Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company corrupts good character.’” (1 Corinthians 15:33). The company they keep does matter, according to him. Keep an eye on who's in your kitchen.
Right. Paul says, “Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company corrupts good character.’” (1 Corinthians 15:33). So company does have an effect on character. That's the warning in his words.

explanations.answer: Some of them are ignorant of God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives. “Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God.” (1 Corinthians 15:34). He says it plainly, friend. That's why the wake-up call is so loud.

explanations.answer: Some of them are leaving the church
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. His reason is that some of them are ignorant of God (1 Corinthians 15:34). Nothing about leaving in that verse.

explanations.answer: Some of them are too proud to pray
explanations.explanation: Pride and prayer aren't what Paul brings up, friend. He says, “…for some of you are ignorant of God.” (1 Corinthians 15:34). That's the reason in the text.
